articleSummary:
- On 3 November 2026, the United States imposes an Ebola-related entry control: from 11:59 PM ET, all passengers on flights to the United States must sign a declaration certifying they have not been physically in the Democratic Republic of the Congo during the previous 21 days. The form, printable or digital, applies to travelers from any country and includes those with layovers in DRC airports, even if they do not disembark. It covers all travelers to the United States—passengers, crew, cargo, general aviation—and also when the U.S. is a connection point to another destination; overflights that do not land are exempt. Each traveller must submit their own declaration; minors may be signed by a parent/guardian. The measure addresses the Ebola outbreak in DRC and is initially valid through 18 
- As of 3 November 2026, Ebola of Bundibugyo lineage is spreading from the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak has exceeded 9,700 cases and 4,680 deaths, into Kenya and Nigeria (first case in Abuja in a woman from Uganda). Supplies are ongoing and complemented by ready-made diagnostics, including PCR tests for monkeypox and Ebola. The program also provides mobile laboratories for rapid threat response, with Russian equipment repaired by Rospotrebnadzor specialists when needed, and distributes protective equipment. The report highlights a Russia–Africa Summit meeting between Vladimir Putin and Ghanaian President John Dramani Mahama, where Mahama thanked Russia for Sputnik V vaccines. The piece also notes Russia’s flu vaccination campaign, reporting over 35.4 million Russians vaccinated to date.

articleHeadline: Why Do We Still Have Malaria? Everyday Practices Undermining Ghana's Fight Against the Disease
articleSummary: Ghana's malaria challenge persists as of 3 November 2026 despite investments in nets, testing, medicines and education. Malaria remains a major public-health burden; transmission is driven by mosquitoes and by poor sanitation, inconsistent net use, self-medication, and limited community participation. Blocked gutters, discarded containers and other water collections create mosquito breeding sites when left unmanaged. Net ownership is insufficient without consistent use, especially by children and pregnant women who are most vulnerable. Self-medication and skipping testing delay diagnosis and proper treatment. Prevention requires collective action: keep drains clear, cover water containers, sleep under nets, seek testing for fevers, and complete prescribed courses. Government should strengthen sanitation, expand net access and testing, and bolster community education and vector-control.

articleHeadline: A study tracking cholera transmission networks in Africa and determining the chances of its spread between countries - Step News Agency
articleSummary: An integrated genomic-epidemiologic study of cholera in Africa analyzes 1762 genomes from 36 countries (1989–2023) and surveillance data from 45 nations (1970–2023). Published in Science, it identifies regional transmission units: two in West Africa and neighbors, a central-east-southern corridor, and a southern cluster; broader epidemiology supports two networks (West Africa and central-to-southern Africa). Transmission declines with distance (88% per 1000 km), but within-unit spread is ~13.5 times higher than between units. AFR10 and AFR9 lineages account for ~46% of Africa’s cholera cases since 1970 (~2.4 million). A Hidden Markov Model combines clinical and genomic data to estimate spread during sampling gaps. Simulations (2000 imports per country) show within-unit outbreaks ~10x likelier in a year; Ghana could seed 4.69 more West African countries, Nigeria 4.33, Cameroon 0.58. Implication: prioritize vaccination in Mozambique if Angola’s outbreak spreads, reflecting network connectivity. Limitations include sampling bias and reliance on suspected cases.

articleHeadline: Zambia Plans 20 Million-Dose Cholera Vaccine Plant Under Agreement with Chinese Firm
articleSummary: Zambia's IDC and China's Jijia International Medical Technology signed a US$24.13 million joint venture to establish ZAMVAX Limited, a vaccine-fill-and-finish facility in Lusaka's South Multi-Facility Economic Zone with capacity to produce up to 20 million oral cholera vaccine doses annually using imported bulk antigen. The broader project totals about US$213 million, with a second phase to introduce local antigen production and possible expansion into pediatric and animal vaccines; IDC will hold 60% and Jijia 40%. The first phase covers filling, finishing, packaging and quality control, not full local vaccine production. Groundbreaking is expected soon; financing, site prep, tech agreements, workforce development and regulatory approvals will follow. The plan addresses vaccine-supply vulnerabilities noted during the Nov 2025 cholera outbreak (957 cases, 20 deaths by Feb 2026). IDC/Jijia will provide technology transfer and training, creating skilled jobs and opportunities for local suppliers.
